title: Phenology-Informed Species Distribution Forecasts for Montane Taxa
content:
Phenology, the timing of events such as leaf-out, flowering and bird migration, responds strongly to temperature and offers an early indicator of ecological change. The study was funded through an institutional grant, and the funder had no role in the design of the methods or the interpretation of the results. Prior work in this area has produced useful results, yet comparisons across studies remain difficult because of differences in data, model structure, and reporting practice. Conservation managers need forecasts of where species will persist, in order to prioritise protected areas and corridors. Long-term monitoring and citizen science records provide the occurrence and phenology data on which most species distribution forecasts depend. Species distribution models relate occurrence records to environmental predictors and are increasingly projected forward to forecast shifts in habitat suitability. Near-term iterative forecasts of ecosystems are updated as new observations arrive, which allows forecasts to be tested and improved within a few years.

Phenology was modelled with a growing degree day approach, calibrated on observed first flowering and first flight dates. Detection probability was estimated from repeat visits so that false absences did not bias the species distribution models. We fitted an ensemble of species distribution models, including a boosted regression tree, a generalised additive model and a maximum entropy model. A held-out portion of the data was reserved for validation and was not used for any tuning decision in the study. The study protocol was written before the analysis began, and departures from it are listed explicitly in the supplementary material. Community science observations were weighted by observer experience to reduce the effect of variable data quality. Iterative forecasting cycles updated the parameters each year with new survey observations through a simple Bayesian updating scheme.

Phenology-informed forecasts predicted occupancy at the upper elevation margins more accurately than static species distribution models. Iterative updating reduced forecast error for first flowering date by about one third after four annual cycles. Habitat suitability was forecast to shift upslope for most species, with the loss of suitable area greatest for the narrowest specialists. Citizen science records improved spatial coverage but introduced detectability biases that the occupancy model only partly absorbed. The results were stable across the sensitivity analyses described in the methods, with only small changes in the central estimates. The ensemble of species distribution models showed good discrimination, though predictions for rare species were poorly calibrated. Differences between the main model and the comparison models were modest in most settings, though a few settings showed clear and consistent gaps.

Species distribution forecasts assume that species-environment relationships persist under novel climates, an assumption that is hard to test. Ecological forecast uncertainty arises from the observation process, from uncertain driver projections, from parameter estimates and from unmodelled biotic interactions. Phenology forecasts carried wide intervals in years of extreme spring temperature, when the growing degree day relationship is poorly constrained. Dispersal limitation and biotic interactions are rarely represented, so predicted suitable habitat may overstate the area species can occupy. Uncertainty in the results arises from several sources, including the data, the model structure, and the choices made during analysis. A limitation of the study is that some sources of uncertainty could not be quantified and are therefore described only qualitatively.

Collaboration with land managers shaped the forecast products so that they are useful for planning reserve boundaries. Near-term iterative ecological forecasting can link monitoring programmes directly to management decisions on a timescale that supports learning. The authors thank the staff of the participating institutions and the anonymous reviewers whose comments improved the study. Taken together, the results suggest that the approach is useful, although further study with additional data would strengthen the conclusions. Community science will remain central to ecological forecasting, provided that detection effects are modelled explicitly. We recommend that monitoring networks publish forecasts and evaluate them openly each season.
